beats.note: walk with them and let it come up
beats.text:
{N} has been getting letters. You have not seen anybody deliver one. They are always on top of the pack in the morning, always folded the same way, and the paper is better than anything sold in the towns you have been walking through.

'Old employer,' they say, folding it away. 'There is paperwork. There is always paperwork.'

You ask whether they are going to read it. {N} says they already have, which does not answer the question you asked, and goes to see about the fire.

beats.note: keep them in fights and see what slips
beats.text:
{N} stops mid-swing and apologises to nobody in particular. The thing they were about to hit takes the opportunity, and the fight goes on around them for a moment while they stand there looking, briefly and unmistakably, embarrassed.

Afterwards, unprompted: 'Not to you. There is a clause about enthusiasm and I am told I have been exceeding it.'

'Told by whom.'

'That is also in the clause,' says {N}, and starts cleaning their weapon with the particular thoroughness of somebody who has finished a conversation.

beats.note: take them to {P}
beats.text:
{N} regards {P} the way most people regard a dentist, which is to say from a distance, for slightly too long, having already decided to go in.

'This is where I signed. I would like the original back, and I would like to not discuss why on the walk in.'

They check their pack twice on the approach. The letters are in it. All of them, in order, tied with something that is not string.

endings.label: Burn it in front of them
endings.text:
The document goes up fast, the way old paper does, and for a moment the light off it is the brightest thing in {P}.

{N} watches every word of it catch. They do not look away and they do not say anything, and when there is nothing left but the smell they work their jaw like somebody testing a new tooth.

The letters stop. You notice it about a week later, on a morning when the top of the pack is just the top of the pack. Something quieter starts around the same time, and they do not mention it, and neither do you.

endings.label: Sell it back to the estate
endings.text:
The estate pays promptly, which tells you what the contract was worth and, by a short walk, what {N} was worth to them.

{N} takes the news like a professional, which is to say entirely. They ask what the figure was. They do not react to the figure. They ask whether the receipt was made out in their name, and when you say it was, they nod once as though a small thing has been confirmed.

They call you 'employer' for a week afterwards without once making it sound like a compliment.

beats.note: walk with them and let it come up
beats.text:
{N} will not eat in front of anyone. They take their share, thank you for it, and walk out to the edge of the firelight with it, and come back with an empty bowl and nothing to say about the interval.

On the fourth night they explain that it is not a religious thing, it is a scheduling thing.

Then they explain nothing further for two days, and eat at the edge of the firelight, and are perfectly pleasant about everything else.

beats.note: put down {X} where they can count them
beats.text:
{N} counts each {X} out loud as it goes down. Not the way you count enemies, which is quick and quiet and about survival -- slowly, and clearly, and with the number said again afterwards.

At three they stop counting and look relieved in a way that does not suit their face at all.

'Three was the number, then.'

'Three was a number,' says {N}. 'There are others. That one was mine.'

beats.note: take them to {P}
beats.text:
'{P},' says {N}. 'Witnessed here.'

They stop you at the threshold with one hand, not urgently, the way somebody stops you before you walk into a low beam.

'Do not sign anything, do not accept a drink, and whatever else happens, do not compliment the furniture.'

You ask what happens if you compliment the furniture. {N} says that it is not a trap, exactly, and that this is the most reassuring answer they have.

endings.label: Buy out the terms
endings.text:
The sum is large. It is large enough that the purse afterwards feels wrong in the hand, lighter in a way that keeps announcing itself, and the receipt is a small cold weight in your pocket for about an hour before it stops existing.

You check the pocket. There was definitely a receipt. There is definitely no receipt.

{N} does not thank you. They do start eating in front of people, which from them is a speech, and the first time they do it they keep going as though nothing is happening and nobody at the fire says a word.

endings.label: Let it stand
endings.text:
The arrangement continues, and the arrangement pays. Whatever it is, it is prompt, and the coin turns up in denominations nobody in the party can place.

{N} accepts this the way you accept weather. 'It was always going to,' they say. 'That is the shape of it. You do not buy out of the shape of a thing, you buy out of the terms, and the terms are the cheap part.'

They are cheerful for a week, which is much worse.

beats.note: walk with them and let it come up
beats.text:
{N} has started sleeping outside the camp, facing out. Not far out -- eight or ten paces, at the edge of where the light gives up, close enough to be first at anything and far enough to be alone with it.

They say the fire ruins their night vision. This is true.

It is not the reason.

beats.note: walk them into a town and watch
beats.text:
In the street somebody calls {N} by a name you did not hire.

{N} does not turn round, does not break stride, and does not say another word for four streets. When they do speak it is about the road out and the weather on it, in a voice pitched exactly like every other time they have talked about the road out.

Behind you the person who shouted is still standing where they were, watching the pair of you go, and they do not shout again.

beats.note: take them to {P}
beats.text:
{P}. {N} goes quiet a hundred paces out and stays quiet.

They have been quiet before -- on watch, on bad ground, after fights that went longer than they should have. This is not that quiet. This is the quiet of somebody doing arithmetic they already know the answer to.

Then: 'They will be smaller than I remember. Everything is. I would like to get this over with.'

endings.label: Go in with them
endings.text:
It is dark and it smells of animal and old smoke, and every surface in there has been worn smooth by something that was not hands.

Whatever meeting happens in there happens in a language with no words in it. There is a long silence, and then a sound like weather, and then another silence that is a different shape from the first one.

{N} comes out walking differently. Not better or worse -- differently, the way somebody walks who has put down a thing they had stopped noticing they were carrying. They do not explain and you do not ask.

endings.label: Wait outside
endings.text:
You wait. It takes a while. You have time to check your gear twice and to think, at some length, about whether waiting was cowardice or manners, and to fail to settle it.

{N} comes out alone carrying something wrapped. They do not offer to show you and you do not look at the shape of it too closely.

They sell it in the next town without discussion, at a counter you would not have chosen, for a figure you would not have accepted, and hand you the larger half. Neither of you raises the subject again.

threads.title: The Favour They Cannot Ask For

beats.note: walk with them and let it come up
beats.text:
{N} cannot lie, as they mention often, in sentences built with the care of a load-bearing wall. Every clause holds up something. Nothing is ever quite the thing you asked about, and every word of it is true.

Tonight one of them fails halfway through. You watch it happen -- the sentence going out over open ground with no support under it -- and so do they.

They sit down in the road. Not dramatically. The way you sit down when your leg has decided the matter for you.

beats.note: keep them in fights and see what slips
beats.text:
'I am glad you are alive,' says {N} after the fight, and then stands very still, apparently checking whether it went through unchallenged.

Nothing objects. The wind carries on. Somewhere behind you somebody is being sick in a hedge.

'Right,' says {N}, to themselves, and writes it down. You did not know they wrote things down.

beats.note: take them to {P}
beats.text:
At {P} something is owed to {N} that they are not permitted to ask for, on account of asking being a kind of lying if you already know the answer.

They have explained this three times on the walk in, each time from a different angle, each time ending slightly earlier than the last.

Now they are standing in front of it and they look at you meaningfully. That is the whole of it. That is the entire mechanism of the thing, and it has been the entire mechanism for longer than you have known them.

endings.label: Ask on their behalf
endings.text:
You ask. It is a small thing, said out loud, and it takes about four seconds.

The thing at {P} hands it over with the bad grace of a clerk at closing, and there is a moment where the whole arrangement is visible: how long this has been waiting, and how little it needed, and how completely {N} could not do it.

{N} does not thank you, because that would also be a kind of lying, and instead is unbearably pleasant for a month.

endings.label: Make them find the words
endings.text:
It takes {N} most of an hour and it is not comfortable to watch.

They start four times. Twice they get far enough that you think it is going to hold, and both times something in the middle of the sentence gives way and they stop, and stand there, and begin again from a different word.

What they eventually construct is technically true, structurally magnificent, and answered without comment by something heavy and unpleasantly warm. {N} looks at it, and then at you, and insists you take half.

beats.note: walk with them and let it come up
beats.text:
{N} keeps a jar. The jar, in a sense they decline to unpack, also keeps {N}.

It is corked. It is always the last thing packed and the first thing checked, and on the two occasions the pack has gone over on bad ground {N} has been off the road and kneeling before anybody else registered the noise.

Asked what is in it, they say 'not much now'.

beats.note: put down {X} where they can see
beats.text:
{N} holds the jar up to each {X} as it falls, the way you show a child a parade. Both hands. Level with their own eyes, and then a little higher.

'He would have liked that one,' they say, of nobody you have met.

It is not said sadly. That is the part you keep turning over afterwards: it is said the way you would pass on a joke to somebody in the next room.

beats.note: take them to {P}
beats.text:
'{P},' says {N}, and sets the jar down on a rock with enormous care, and then adjusts it, and then adjusts it back.

'He asked to be brought here. He asked a lot of things. Most of them were about the tide, and about whether I had eaten, and about a man called Ardal who I have never been able to find.'

They straighten up. 'This is the one I can still do.'

endings.label: Help them bury it
endings.text:
The ground is bad and it takes both of you the better part of the afternoon. Twice you hit rock and start again a pace to the left, and {N} does not once suggest that anywhere else would do.

When it is deep enough they say a few words that are mostly logistics -- where this is, how far it is from the water, what the weather is doing.

Afterwards they are lighter by about a jar, and by rather more than that.

endings.label: Tell them to keep it
endings.text:
{N} thinks about it for a long moment. The rock is right there and so is the jar and so, for that matter, is the afternoon.

Then they pack it away again, visibly relieved and visibly ashamed of being relieved, and are noticeably brisk about getting back on the road.

Somebody in the next town pays absurdly well for a look at it. {N} negotiates. {N} is *good* at negotiating, which is new information. You split that.

beats.note: walk with them and let it come up
beats.text:
{N} has been counting their own steps since the day you hired them and will tell you the number if asked.

It is correct. It has been correct every time you have checked, including the time you counted a thousand of them yourself out of pure suspicion and lost your place twice and had to take their word for the remainder anyway.

They do not appear to be concentrating on it. They do it while talking, while eating, and, as far as anyone can establish, while asleep.

beats.note: walk them into a town and watch
beats.text:
A man in a good coat follows you for two streets, writing. He is not subtle about it and he is not nervous about it either, which between them are worse than one or the other.

He leaves when {N} looks at him. Not hurriedly. He finishes the line first.

'They keep notes,' {N} says. 'I would quite like to read them. I am the subject.'

beats.note: take them to {P}
beats.text:
The notes are at {P}, in a box, in an order somebody thought about. The box is not locked. That is somehow the worst detail available: whoever filled it never expected the subject to come and collect.

{N} stands in front of it with their hands behind their back like a person at a graveside, and does not reach for it, and does not move.

'Nineteen years of somebody else's opinion of me,' they say. 'It is a lot to have in a box.'

endings.label: Burn the notes unread
endings.text:
{N} does not read a page of it, which you suspect took more out of them than the walk did.

They lift the box, they hold it for a moment at arm's length as though weighing something that is not its weight, and then it goes on the fire whole. The fire is brief and thorough. The box burns better than the paper does.

'Now nobody has established what,' they say, apparently pleased. 'Including me.'

endings.label: Sell them to the college
endings.text:
The college pays without haggling, which is how you learn what {N} is worth on paper.

They pay in one go, in front of witnesses, and the man who counts it out does not once look at {N}, who is standing next to you the entire time being extremely polite to everybody.

{N} reads the receipt with great interest and asks to keep it. They are noticeably easier company afterwards and noticeably more expensive, and if there is a connection between those two things they have not offered it.

beats.note: walk with them and let it come up
beats.text:
{N} counts their cut twice every time. Once when you hand it over and once again later, out of sight, when they think nobody is looking -- and they are wrong about that, because you have been watching people count money for a living for some time now.

Most of it goes somewhere that is not a pocket.

Asked about it, they say 'it is spoken for' in the voice of somebody quoting.

beats.note: keep them in fights and see what slips
beats.text:
{N} takes a bad hit and says a name on the way down.

It is not yours and it is not theirs. It is two syllables, and it is said the way you say a name to somebody who is in the room.

When they get up they are extremely keen to talk about anything else, and they talk about anything else for the rest of the day, at length, on subjects they have never previously shown any interest in whatsoever.

beats.note: take them to {P}
beats.text:
The sum is owed in {P}, and has been for long enough to have grown a personality.

{N} lays it out on the walk in with the flatness of a bill of lading: how much, since when, to whom, and what has been added to it since by people who were entitled to add things.

They are very calm about all of this, in the way of somebody who has rehearsed being calm about it, on the road, alone, more than once.

endings.label: Settle it out of the purse
endings.text:
The debt is smaller than the dread of it, which is how debts work.

{N} watches it get paid. They watch the whole transaction, every stage of it, including the part where the clerk rules a line through the entry and blots it, and they do not say anything until it is done.

Then they say 'right'. And then, about ten minutes later, out on the road, to nobody, they say 'right' again.

endings.label: Introduce yourself to the creditor
endings.text:
You have a conversation. It is not a long one and nothing is broken.

The creditor is a reasonable person who has been dealing with an unreasonable situation for some years and who has, you get the strong impression, been dreading this meeting rather more than {N} has.

The terms afterwards are extremely reasonable. {N} looks at you for the rest of the day as though recalculating something, and asks, once, quite carefully, what exactly you said.

beats.note: walk with them and let it come up
beats.text:
{N} asks, casually, whether {X} ever drops {I}.

Then asks again the next day, and the day after that, each time as though for the first, each time with the same studied lack of interest and the same half-second pause before the question.

On the fourth day you say yes, sometimes. {N} says 'huh', and does not ask again for a week, which is how you know it was the answer they wanted.

beats.note: put down {X} until they say when
beats.text:
Three of them down, and {N} has been through all three with a knife and an expression of mounting professional disappointment.

'Not that one either.'

They clean the knife. They are not sulking -- it is worse than sulking, it is patient, and it is the patience of somebody who has done this on their own for years and has an unexamined amount of time budgeted for doing it on their own for years more.

beats.note: take them to {P}
beats.text:
'The big one is at {P},' says {N}.

'It has been at {P} for eleven years. I have been not going to {P} for eleven years. Those two facts are related.'

They say it looking at the horizon rather than at you, and then they check their gear, which they checked an hour ago, and then they check it again.

endings.label: Let them take the shot
endings.text:
{N} takes it.

It is not clean and it is not quick and nobody says anything encouraging while it is happening, because the one thing you can see clearly from where you are standing is that encouragement would be an insult.

Afterwards they hold up {I} in both hands and look at it for a very long time. Long enough that you start to wonder. Then they put it in a pocket like a receipt, and say that they should like to get moving before dark.

endings.label: Take it yourself and hand it over
endings.text:
You do it. It is easier than it should be, and that is the problem.

{N} is grateful, thoroughly and out loud, in front of everybody, at a length that goes past the point where you can enjoy it and out the other side.

Something goes out of them that you cannot put back. They ask for a bigger share the following week and you give it, and you would have given it anyway, and both of you know that.

beats.note: walk them into a town and watch
beats.text:
{N} does not go into the tavern.

{N} waits outside the tavern, at an angle, with a view of both doors, and does it so naturally that it takes you three towns to notice it is a habit rather than a preference.

Asked, they give a reason. It is a decent reason. It is unable to survive being said out loud, and both of you hear it fail, and neither of you says so.

beats.note: walk with them and let it come up
beats.text:
The name you hired {N} under is on a list somewhere, they explain, along with a description that is unfair and a sum that is not.

The description, they say, has them a head taller and considerably better looking, which they have decided to be annoyed about on principle.

The sum is the part they resent. 'It is not even a good sum. I have done things worth a great deal more than that and they were not on the list at all.'

beats.note: take them to {P}
beats.text:
The list is kept in {P}, and so is the man who keeps it.

{N} points this out on the road in, in the tone of somebody remarking on the crop rotation, and then waits an entire mile before adding: 'I am not asking. I am describing a situation.'

You point out that they have described the situation four times. {N} agrees that they have.

endings.label: Have the name struck off
endings.text:
It costs what it costs and the clerk does not look up once, which is either professional discretion or complete indifference and is, for your purposes, identical.

{N} reads the amended page twice. Then they mouth their own name off it, silently, the way you check a word you have only ever seen written down.

They are unreasonably good company for a fortnight, and they go into the next tavern first.

endings.label: Have it sold to somebody else
endings.text:
There is always a market for a name with a sum attached, and it turns out there is a fairly brisk one.

The buyer is delighted. The clerk is incurious. The whole thing takes less time than the argument about whether to do it.

{N} is now legally somebody with a much worse reputation and considerably more money, and spends the walk out trying on the new name in different tones of voice to see which of them they can stand.

beats.note: come back when you have seen a few
beats.text: {N} does not introduce themselves. '{X},' they say. 'You have seen one. I can tell, you have the look.' They tap the floorboards twice with a heel. 'There is one under here. Has been for eleven years. It pays rent.'

beats.note: put down four of {X}, then go back to {N}
beats.text: 'Four,' says {N}, counting on fingers that have done this before. 'Four is enough to know. They do not scream, do they. They just stop.' A long pause. 'Mine screams. So either mine is different, or the rest of them are being polite.'

endings.label: Go down and look
endings.text: The cellar is dry and cold and entirely empty except for a chair, which is warm. {N} takes this news standing up, then sits down on the floor of their own kitchen and stays there a while. 'Eleven years,' they say. 'I could have just gone down.'

endings.label: Tell them it is nothing
endings.text: 'Nothing,' repeats {N}, and you can watch them decide to believe it. They pay you for the trouble out of a tin kept for exactly this, which suggests you are not the first. The floorboards do not come up.

beats.note: go to {P}, then come back and tell {N}
beats.text: 'You will be going out that way,' says {N}. It is not a question. 'My brother went to {P}. Eight months ago. He was not a brave man, which is why I have not gone to look — I am the one he got it from.'

beats.note: go to {P}, then come back and tell {N}
beats.text: There is a name scratched into the wall by the entrance, and under it, in the same hand and a great deal deeper, a second attempt at the same name. Nothing else in the place has been touched in years.

endings.label: Tell them exactly what you found
endings.text: {N} listens to all of it, including the part about the second scratch, and does not cry until you have finished, which you suspect was deliberate. Then they feed you, at length, and refuse every coin you offer, also at length.

endings.label: Tell them he made it further than that
endings.text: It costs you nothing to say and {N} takes hold of it with both hands. They tell the neighbours. The neighbours tell people. Somewhere out there is a version of that brother who died gloriously, and it is doing very well for itself.

beats.note: come back through here when you have been out a while
beats.text: 'You are the fourth person through this month,' says {N}, 'so I will say it to you as well.' They put a wrapped parcel on the counter. 'Paid for in advance, eleven years ago, by somebody who said they would be back on the Thursday. Which Thursday was not specified.'

beats.note: go and be somewhere else for a while, then come back
beats.text: The parcel is on the counter again, in exactly the same place, and {N} has clearly been putting it away and getting it out. '{I},' they say, before you ask. 'That is what is in it. I looked, in year six. I have felt terrible ever since and I would do it again.'

endings.label: Buy it off them
endings.text: {N} takes the money like somebody being talked down off a ledge, and puts the parcel into your hands with both of theirs. 'If he comes back,' they say, 'I will send him to you.' The counter looks enormous now, and empty.

endings.label: Tell them to keep waiting
endings.text: 'Right,' says {N}. 'Right.' The parcel goes back under the counter. They are visibly relieved, which is the worst part of the whole exchange, and they insist on paying you for the conversation.

beats.note: let them get another look at you
beats.text: {N} watches you the whole way across the room and carries on after you have stopped being interesting. 'You are not from here either,' they say eventually. 'Do not worry. Nobody has worked out that I am not, and I have had nineteen years to give myself away.'

beats.note: come back through this town again
beats.text: 'Nineteen years,' says {N}, picking it up as though no time has passed, which for them it has not. 'I have a whole family here. They think I am from the coast. I am not from the coast. I have never seen the coast.' They look at you levelly. 'You have been out. Is it there?'

endings.label: Tell them what is out there
endings.text: You describe it. {N} takes it in the way somebody takes a diagnosis — carefully, and without interrupting once. At the end they say 'good' twice, meaning it differently each time, and go back to work with the look of a person who has stopped waiting for something.

endings.label: Ask what they are hiding from
endings.text: {N} tells you. It takes a while, none of it is your business, and by the end you are holding a good deal more of it than you meant to. There is money involved, historically, and some of it is still in a box under a floor in this town.
